questions.question: The Supreme Court can issue writs under Article 32 only for which specific purpose?

options.text: To review decisions of statutory tribunals
To enforce the Directive Principles of State Policy

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To protect Fundamental Rights**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 32 of the Indian Constitution provides the right to Constitutional Remedies, empowering the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• Writs under Article 32 include Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari, ensuring the protection of Fundamental Rights.
 
• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, emphasizing its significance in safeguarding citizens' rights.
 
• Only the Supreme Court can issue writs under Article 32, while High Courts can issue writs under Article 226 for broader purposes, including legal rights.
 
• Article 32 is considered a cornerstone of the judiciary's role in maintaining checks and balances in India's democratic framework.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:** These are guaranteed under Part III of the Indian Constitution and include rights such as the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• **Types of Writs:**
 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** To release a person unlawfully detained.
 
• **Mandamus:** To compel a public authority to perform its legal duty.
 
• **Prohibition:** To prevent lower courts from exceeding their jurisdiction.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** To challenge the legality of a person's claim to a public office.
 
• **Certiorari:** To transfer a case from lower courts to higher courts for review.
 
 
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy:** Mentioned under Part IV of the Constitution, these are non-justiciable guidelines for the government to ensure social and economic welfare.
 
• **Judicial Review:** Under Article 13, the judiciary has the power to invalidate laws that violate Fundamental Rights, ensuring their supremacy.
 
• **Comparison with Article 226:** Article 226 allows High Courts to issue writs not only for Fundamental Rights but also for legal rights, making its scope broader than Article 32.

questions.question: Which type of subordinate court primarily handles disputes related to property ownership and contractual agreements?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Civil Courts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Civil Courts** primarily handle disputes related to property ownership, contractual agreements, and other civil matters.
 
• They deal with cases involving disputes over land, property partition, inheritance, and breach of contracts.
 
• Civil courts operate under the **Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908**, which governs their functioning in India.
 
• The hierarchy of civil courts includes **District Courts, Subordinate Courts, and Small Causes Courts**, depending on the value and nature of disputes.
 
• The jurisdiction of civil courts varies based on the **monetary value and territorial limits** of the case in question.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revenue Courts**:

 
 
• These courts primarily handle cases related to **land revenue**, tenancy disputes, and agricultural land issues.
 
• They function under various state-specific revenue laws and are not concerned with property ownership disputes unless related to revenue matters.
 
 
 
• **Criminal Courts**:
 
 
• Criminal courts deal with offenses against the state, such as theft, assault, murder, and other crimes punishable under the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
 
• They do not handle civil matters like property disputes or contractual disagreements.
 
 
 
• **Family Courts**:
 
 
• These courts specialize in handling cases related to **marriage, divorce, child custody, and maintenance**.
 
• They are governed by the Family Courts Act, 1984, and do not address property or contract-related disputes.
 
 
 
• **Small Causes Courts**:
 
 
• These courts deal with cases of **minor civil disputes**, such as unpaid bills, rents, or small contract violations, typically involving a lower monetary value.
 
• They have limited jurisdiction compared to regular civil courts.

questions.question: Which Article of the Directive Principles of State Policy was added by the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 43 B**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 43 B** was added to the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) by the **97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011**.
 
• This Article aims to **promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of cooperative societies**.
 
• The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act recognizes **cooperatives** as an important economic vehicle for inclusive growth.
 
• It inserts the word **"cooperatives"** in Article 19(1)(c), ensuring the right to form cooperative societies as a fundamental right.
 
• Additionally, Article 43 B in Part IV of the Constitution emphasizes the state's role in promoting cooperatives.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **97th Constitutional Amendment Act:**

 
 
• It came into effect on **15 February 2012**.
 
• The amendment added **"cooperative societies"** to the Constitution, recognizing their significance in economic development.
 
• It made provisions for the **protection and regulation of cooperative societies** under state law.
 
 
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy:**
 
 
• These principles are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They are non-justiciable but serve as guidelines for the government in policy-making.
 
• The DPSPs aim to establish a welfare state, ensuring socio-economic justice.
 
 
 
• **Cooperative Societies:**
 
 
• Cooperatives are **autonomous associations** of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social, and cultural needs.
 
• They are based on principles such as **democratic control and equitable distribution of resources**.
 
• In India, cooperatives play a crucial role in sectors like agriculture, banking, and housing.
 
 
 
• **Part IV of the Constitution:**
 
 
• Part IV of the Constitution deals with **Directive Principles of State Policy**.
 
• It includes Articles 36 to 51, focusing on principles to be followed by the state to ensure the welfare of citizens.
 
• Articles such as 38, 39, 41, and 43 highlight socio-economic goals like equal pay, living wages, and right to work.

questions.question: Which urban local self government body manages small towns with limited municipal functions like street lighting and drainage?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Town Area Committee**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A **Town Area Committee** is a semi-municipal authority responsible for administering small towns with limited municipal functions.
 
• It typically manages essential services such as **street lighting, drainage, and sanitation** in areas that are not large enough to require a full-fledged municipal corporation.
 
• These committees are constituted by the **State Governments** and operate under their supervision.
 
• Unlike municipal corporations, a Town Area Committee has **limited jurisdiction and fewer responsibilities**.
 
• The members of the committee can be either **elected, nominated, or both**, depending on state regulations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Municipal Corporation:**

 
 
• A municipal corporation is an urban local government body responsible for the governance of large cities with populations exceeding a specific threshold (e.g., 1 lakh or more).
 
• It handles diverse functions such as waste management, public transportation, and urban planning.
 
 
 
• **Special Purpose Agencies:**
 
 
• These are autonomous bodies created to manage specific functions like water supply, transportation, or housing in urban areas.
 
• They operate independently of the municipal government.
 
 
 
• **Port Trust:**
 
 
• A Port Trust is a specialized body responsible for managing and maintaining ports and their associated facilities.
 
• It primarily focuses on trade and maritime operations rather than urban governance.
 
 
 
• **Urban Local Self-Government:**
 
 
• Urban local self-government refers to the institutions that govern cities and towns, ensuring the provision of essential services and infrastructure.
 
• Examples include municipal corporations, municipalities, town area committees, and notified area councils.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction in federal disputes versus its writ jurisdiction?

options.text: Federal dispute jurisdiction is exclusive to SC, while writ jurisdiction is concurrent with High Courts.
Federal dispute jurisdiction can be exercised suo moto, while writ jurisdiction requires a petition.
Federal dispute jurisdiction applies to civil matters, while writ jurisdiction applies to criminal matters.
Federal dispute jurisdiction is advisory, while writ jurisdiction is binding.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Federal dispute jurisdiction is exclusive to SC, while writ jurisdiction is concurrent with High Courts.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Federal Dispute Jurisdiction**: It is exclusive to the Supreme Court under Article 131 of the Indian Constitution. This means no other court, including High Courts, can exercise jurisdiction in such disputes.
 
• **Writ Jurisdiction**: The writ jurisdiction under Article 32 is concurrent, meaning both the Supreme Court and High Courts can issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
 
• The key distinction is exclusivity—federal disputes under original jurisdiction are solely handled by the Supreme Court, whereas writ jurisdiction is shared between the Supreme Court and High Courts.
 
• The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in federal disputes includes cases between the Government of India and one or more states or between states themselves.
 
• Writ jurisdiction pertains to safeguarding fundamental rights and can be invoked by individuals or groups through petitions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 131 (Original Jurisdiction of SC):** Deals with disputes involving the Central Government and one or more states, or between states themselves, ensuring a direct and exclusive mechanism for resolving federal disputes.
 
• **Article 32 (Writ Jurisdiction of SC):** Known as the “heart and soul of the Constitution” by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, it empowers individuals to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcing fundamental rights via writs.
 
• **Types of Writs:** Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto are the five writs available under both Articles 32 (Supreme Court) and 226 (High Courts).
 
• **Concurrent Jurisdiction:** High Courts under Article 226 can issue writs for both fundamental rights and other purposes, making their jurisdiction broader compared to the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction.
 
• **Federalism in India:** The exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in federal disputes highlights the need for a neutral arbiter to resolve conflicts between different levels of government.

questions.question: What happens if an Indian citizen voluntarily becomes a citizen of another country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Their Indian citizenship ends automatically**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• As per the **Indian Citizenship Act, 1955**, Indian citizenship is automatically terminated when an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country.
 
• India follows the principle of **single citizenship**, meaning that dual citizenship is not allowed under Indian law.
 
• An individual acquiring foreign citizenship must **surrender their Indian passport** as it becomes invalid after acquiring foreign nationality.
 
• The government of India issues an **Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card** to eligible individuals of Indian origin, which provides certain privileges but is not equivalent to dual citizenship.
 
• Section 9(1) of the Indian Citizenship Act explicitly states that **Indian citizenship ceases automatically** upon acquiring foreign citizenship voluntarily.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian Citizenship Act, 1955**

 
 
• This act governs the acquisition, termination, and supplementary provisions of Indian citizenship.
 
• It provides five modes of acquiring citizenship: by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
 
• It also lays down the grounds for the termination and deprivation of citizenship under specific conditions.
 
 
 
• **Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) Card**
 
 
• The OCI card is issued to foreign nationals of Indian origin, allowing them to visit, live, or work in India indefinitely.
 
• It is not equivalent to Indian citizenship, and OCI cardholders cannot vote, hold government office, or purchase agricultural land in India.
 
• The scheme was introduced in 2005 to strengthen the bond between India and its diaspora.
 
 
 
• **Dual Citizenship**
 
 
• Dual citizenship refers to a situation where an individual is a legal citizen of two countries simultaneously.
 
• India does not allow dual citizenship; instead, it provides the OCI card as an alternative for individuals of Indian origin.
 
 
 
• **Surrender Certificate**
 
 
• Indian citizens who acquire foreign nationality must obtain a surrender certificate for their Indian passport.
 
• This certificate is required for availing of consular services and applying for an OCI card.

questions.question: After the 97th Constitutional Amendment, for how long can a state co-operative law that is inconsistent with the amendment remain in force?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 year**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 97th Constitutional Amendment introduced reforms to promote the autonomy and democratic functioning of cooperative societies in India.
 
• Under this amendment, state laws inconsistent with the provisions of the amendment can remain in force for a maximum period of **1 year** from the commencement of the amendment.
 
• This period allows states to make necessary modifications to their cooperative laws to comply with the amendment.
 
• The amendment aimed to make cooperative societies more accountable, transparent, and member-driven.
 
• It also added a new part, Part IXB, to the Constitution of India to specifically deal with cooperative societies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **97th Constitutional Amendment:**

 
 
• The amendment was passed in 2011 and came into effect on February 15, 2012.
 
• It added Article 43B to the Directive Principles of State Policy, encouraging states to promote voluntary formation, democratic functioning, and professional management of cooperative societies.
 
 
 
• **Part IXB of the Constitution:**
 
 
• This part specifically deals with cooperative societies and outlines provisions for their governance.
 
• It includes provisions for the composition, election, and tenure of the board of cooperative societies.
 
 
 
• **Objective of the Amendment:**
 
 
• To improve the functioning of cooperative societies and ensure their accountability to members.
 
• To protect the interests of members and prevent misuse of funds and powers.
 
 
 
• **Legal Framework:**
 
 
• States were required to amend their cooperative society laws to comply with the constitutional provisions within one year.
 
• Any inconsistent state law beyond this period would cease to have effect.

questions.question: What percentage of seats are reserved for women under the 106th Amendment Act?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**33%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 106th Amendment Act of the Indian Constitution proposed **33% reservation for women in Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.**
 
• This amendment aimed to ensure gender equality in political representation and decision-making bodies.
 
• The reservation was to apply to both directly elected seats and seats reserved for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs).
 
• The bill to enact this amendment was commonly referred to as the **Women's Reservation Bill**.
 
• Though widely discussed and debated, the bill has not been implemented as of the latest updates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Women's Reservation Bill:**

 
 
• Introduced in Parliament in **1996**, it aimed to reserve 33% of seats for women in Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.
 
• The bill was passed in the Rajya Sabha in 2010 but has not been passed in the Lok Sabha.
 
• The aim was to enhance women’s participation in governance and policy-making.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Women's Representation:**
 
 
• Increased representation of women ensures diverse perspectives in decision-making.
 
• It promotes gender equality and empowers women politically, socially, and economically.
 
 
 
• **Current Status of Women's Representation:**
 
 
• As of 2023, women constitute approximately **14% of the Lok Sabha and 10% of the State Assemblies**.
 
• India ranks relatively low in the global Gender Gap Index in terms of political empowerment.
 
 
 
• **Global Examples:**
 
 
• Countries like Rwanda and Sweden have implemented effective gender quotas in their legislatures.
 
• Rwanda has over 60% representation of women in its Parliament, the highest in the world.

questions.question: Which schedule allows for the creation of village councils or courts for tribal cases?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sixth Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Sixth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution provides for the **administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram**.
 
• It allows for the establishment of **Autonomous District Councils (ADCs)**, which are empowered to make laws and govern certain aspects of administration in tribal areas.
 
• The ADCs are authorized to create **village councils or courts** for handling disputes and cases involving tribal individuals, ensuring their customary laws and practices are preserved.
 
• This schedule provides a legal framework to protect the rights and culture of tribal communities while granting them **self-governance**.
 
• The Sixth Schedule seeks to empower tribal regions by granting them autonomy in areas such as land use, resource management, and administration of justice.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Autonomous District Councils (ADCs):**

 
 
• ADCs are created under the Sixth Schedule to administer tribal areas and protect tribal rights.
 
• They have the authority to legislate on matters such as land, forests, water, customs, and inheritance.
 
• ADCs are composed of members both elected and nominated by the Governor of the respective state.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Courts:**
 
 
• Village councils or courts established under ADCs are empowered to handle cases involving tribal individuals in accordance with customary laws.
 
• These courts aim to ensure quick and culturally sensitive resolution of disputes within tribal communities.
 
 
 
• **Other Schedules Related to Tribals:**
 
 
• The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in other states (excluding the Sixth Schedule states).
 
• The Sixth Schedule, however, provides a more autonomous framework for certain northeastern states.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Sixth Schedule:**
 
 
• It preserves the unique cultural identity and traditions of tribal communities.
 
• It ensures self-governance and participatory democracy within tribal areas.

questions.question: When was the Protection of Human Rights Act passed in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1993**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Protection of Human Rights Act** was enacted in India in **1993** to provide for the establishment of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC).
 
• The Act aims to protect and promote human rights in accordance with the Constitution of India and international human rights instruments.
 
• The **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)** was constituted under this Act as an independent statutory body.
 
• The Act also provides for the formation of **State Human Rights Commissions** to address human rights issues at the state level.
 
• The Act defines "human rights" as rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Human Rights Commission (NHRC):**

 
 
• Established in October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
 
• It consists of a Chairperson and other members appointed by the President of India.
 
• The Commission investigates complaints of human rights violations and provides recommendations to the government.
 
 
 
• **State Human Rights Commissions:**
 
 
• Each state in India can establish its own Human Rights Commission under the Act.
 
• These bodies address human rights issues specific to their respective states.
 
 
 
• **International Human Rights Instruments:**
 
 
• India is a signatory to major human rights treaties such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR).
 
• The Protection of Human Rights Act aligns with international standards to safeguard human rights.
 
 
 
• **Amendments to the Act:**
 
 
• The Act has been amended several times to strengthen the functioning of NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions.
 
• The latest amendment was made in 2019 to include changes in the composition and tenure of members.

questions.question: Which institution has been established by the 74th Constitutional Amendment, 1992, to conduct municipal elections in each State?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**State Election Commission**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, mandated the establishment of the **State Election Commission** in every state to conduct elections to municipalities and panchayati raj institutions.
 
• The State Election Commission is empowered to supervise, direct, and control the entire process of municipal and local body elections.
 
• The amendment added **Part IX-A** to the Constitution, specifically dealing with municipalities and urban local governance.
 
• Article **243K** of the Constitution provides for the State Election Commission and specifies its role in conducting free and fair elections at the local level.
 
• The State Election Commission operates independently of the Election Commission of India, focusing solely on elections for local governance bodies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act:**

 
 
• Enacted in **1992**, it aimed to strengthen urban local governance in India.
 
• Introduced three types of municipalities: **Nagar Panchayat**, **Municipal Council**, and **Municipal Corporation**.
 
• It granted municipalities constitutional status, ensuring their establishment and functioning as units of self-governance.
 
 
 
• **State Election Commission:**
 
 
• Established under Article 243K of the Constitution.
 
• The commission is headed by a **State Election Commissioner**, appointed by the Governor of the state.
 
• Its independence is ensured by the constitutional protection of its tenure.
 
 
 
• **Municipal Governance:**
 
 
• Municipalities manage urban areas and provide essential services like sanitation, water supply, and infrastructure development.
 
• Elected representatives, including mayors and councilors, oversee the administration of these local bodies.
 
 
 
• **Article 243K:**
 
 
• Explicitly provides for the establishment of a State Election Commission for conducting local body elections.
 
• Empowers the commission to control and supervise municipal elections.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution explicitly declares laws violating Fundamental Rights as void?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 13**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 13** of the Indian Constitution explicitly declares that any law inconsistent with or violating Fundamental Rights shall be void.
 
• This Article ensures that Fundamental Rights, enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, remain supreme and protected from legislative infringement.
 
• It provides for judicial review, empowering courts to strike down laws that violate Fundamental Rights.
 
• Article 13 classifies laws into two categories: pre-Constitution laws (existing laws before January 26, 1950) and post-Constitution laws.
 
• The judiciary plays a crucial role in interpreting Article 13 to ensure the protection of Fundamental Rights, making it a cornerstone of India's constitutional framework.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights** are basic rights guaranteed to all citizens under Part III of the Indian Constitution, ensuring equality, freedom, and protection against arbitrary actions of the state.
 
• **Judicial Review:** A process through which courts assess the validity of laws and executive actions to ensure compliance with the Constitution.
 
• **Doctrine of Eclipse:** Under Article 13, pre-Constitution laws conflicting with Fundamental Rights are not nullified but remain dormant, becoming enforceable if the conflict is removed later.
 
• **Doctrine of Severability:** If a part of a law violates Fundamental Rights, only the offending portion is declared invalid, and the rest remains operational.
 
• **Article 32:** Known as the "Right to Constitutional Remedies," it empowers citizens to approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights.

questions.question: Which criticism highlights the parliamentary system’s departure from the principle of separation of powers?

options.text: The President has absolute control over the Prime Minister.
The cabinet simultaneously leads the executive and legislature, creating fusion of powers.
The executive and legislature operate independently.
Ministers are appointed based on expertise rather than political affiliation.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The cabinet simultaneously leads the executive and legislature, creating fusion of powers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The parliamentary system exhibits a **fusion of powers**, where the executive branch (cabinet) is drawn from and accountable to the legislature.
 
• This fusion of powers departs from the principle of separation of powers, which emphasizes **distinct and independent roles** for the executive, legislature, and judiciary.
 
• Ministers in the cabinet serve dual roles as heads of executive departments and legislators, which can lead to **overlap of functions**.
 
• The Prime Minister and cabinet are directly answerable to the legislature, often blurring the line between the two branches of government.
 
• In contrast, the presidential system follows a stricter separation of powers where the executive and legislature operate independently.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Separation of Powers:**

 
 
• A constitutional principle that divides government responsibilities into three branches: **executive, legislature, and judiciary**.
 
• Ensures no single branch exercises complete control, promoting checks and balances.
 
• The concept was popularized by **Montesquieu** in his work "The Spirit of Laws."
 
 
 
• **Fusion of Powers:**
 
 
• A characteristic of the parliamentary system where the executive and legislature are **interconnected.**
 
• Allows for a unified government but can lead to **less stringent checks and balances**.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary System:**
 
 
• The head of government (Prime Minister) is usually a member of the legislature.
 
• The executive is dependent on the support of the legislature and can be **removed by a vote of no confidence**.
 
• Examples include the systems of the United Kingdom and India.
 
 
 
• **Presidential System:**
 
 
• Features a strict separation of powers between the executive and legislature.
 
• The President is both the head of state and government, elected independently of the legislature.
 
• Examples include the systems of the United States and Brazil.

questions.question: Under the Fifth Schedule, the Governor's regulations in Scheduled Areas can prohibit or restrict which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Land transfers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides special administrative provisions for the Scheduled Areas, primarily to protect the rights of tribal communities.
 
• The Governor of a state with Scheduled Areas is empowered to make regulations to prohibit or restrict the **transfer of land by or among members of Scheduled Tribes**.
 
• These regulations aim to prevent the exploitation of tribal land by non-tribal individuals or entities.
 
• The Governor can also regulate the allotment of land for agricultural purposes or settlement, ensuring the protection of tribal interests.
 
• The objective is to uphold tribal autonomy, safeguard their cultural identity, and prevent land alienation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Scheduled Areas**

 
 
• Scheduled Areas are specified regions in India recognized for the protection of tribal communities under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution.
 
• These areas are identified based on the concentration of tribal populations and their socio-economic backwardness.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Governor**
 
 
• The Governor has legislative authority under the Fifth Schedule to make regulations for peace and good governance in Scheduled Areas.
 
• This includes the power to modify or nullify laws passed by the State Legislature in these areas.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Land Protection**
 
 
• The primary aim of restrictions on land transfers is to prevent the alienation of tribal land to non-tribals, which could lead to loss of livelihood and cultural erosion.
 
• Such measures also help in preserving the unique tribal identity and traditional rights of indigenous communities.
 
 
 
• **Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA)**
 
 
• PESA empowers Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas to safeguard and preserve the traditions, customs, and resources of tribal communities.
 
• It provides for self-governance and the management of natural resources by tribal groups.

questions.question: What happens when an Indian citizen renounces their citizenship?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They lose their Indian citizenship**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Indian citizenship can be renounced voluntarily under the provisions of the **Citizenship Act, 1955**.
 
• Upon renouncing citizenship, the individual ceases to be an Indian citizen and forfeits all rights and privileges associated with Indian nationality.
 
• A declaration of renunciation must be made in the prescribed form and submitted to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
• The individual may acquire citizenship of another country, but dual citizenship is not permitted under Indian law.
 
• Renunciation of citizenship does not absolve individuals of any prior liabilities or responsibilities as an Indian citizen.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Citizenship Act, 1955:**

 
 
• The Citizenship Act, 1955 governs the acquisition, termination, and determination of Indian citizenship.
 
• It provides for citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
 
• Section 8 of the Act deals with voluntary renunciation of citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI):**
 
 
• Although India does not permit dual citizenship, it offers an OCI card for individuals of Indian origin.
 
• The OCI card provides certain rights, such as visa-free travel to India and access to specific rights, but it does not confer full citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Dual Citizenship:**
 
 
• India does not allow dual citizenship under its laws.
 
• Individuals renouncing Indian citizenship may acquire citizenship of another country, but they cannot simultaneously retain Indian citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Consequences of Renouncing Citizenship:**
 
 
• The individual loses voting rights, eligibility for public office, and access to Indian government schemes.
 
• They may also face restrictions on property ownership and legal rights in India.

questions.question: Article 31B was introduced to protect which type of laws from court challenges?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Land reform laws**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 31B was introduced in the Constitution of India through the First Amendment Act of 1951 to provide protection to certain laws from judicial review.
 
• The primary purpose of Article 31B was to safeguard **land reform laws** from being challenged in courts on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights.
 
• Laws listed under the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution are protected by Article 31B, ensuring they cannot be invalidated by courts.
 
• This provision was critical for implementing agrarian reforms and redistributing land to reduce inequalities in rural India.
 
• It was aimed at addressing socio-economic disparities and promoting equitable land ownership among citizens, especially marginalized communities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First Amendment Act, 1951**

 
 
• The First Amendment introduced Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule to protect laws related to land reforms and socio-economic development.
 
• It was enacted under the leadership of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
 
• This amendment was essential to address challenges posed by judicial scrutiny of land redistribution laws.
 
 
 
• **Ninth Schedule of the Constitution**
 
 
• The Ninth Schedule lists laws that are immune from judicial review under Article 31B.
 
• Initially, 13 laws were included in the Ninth Schedule, primarily dealing with land reforms.
 
• Over time, more laws were added, covering various socio-economic measures.
 
 
 
• **Land Reforms in India**
 
 
• Land reforms involved measures such as abolishing zamindari (landlord system) and redistributing land to landless farmers.
 
• These reforms were aimed at reducing rural poverty and fostering agricultural development.
 
• Article 31B ensured these reforms were not obstructed by legal challenges.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review and Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• Article 13 of the Constitution empowers the judiciary to review laws that violate fundamental rights.
 
• Article 31B creates an exception by protecting certain laws listed under the Ninth Schedule from such scrutiny.
 
• This ensures that socio-economic reforms are not impeded by judicial intervention.

questions.question: What happens if a law is declared unconstitutional under judicial review?

options.text: It is sent back to the Parliament for reconsideration.
It is amended by the President

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It becomes null and void.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• If a law is declared unconstitutional under judicial review, it **ceases to have any legal effect** and is treated as if it never existed.
 
• The judiciary exercises this power under the principle of **constitutional supremacy**, ensuring that all laws adhere to the constitution.
 
• Such a declaration is binding on all authorities, including the legislature, executive, and judiciary.
 
• The law is considered **null and void** from the date of its enactment, unless the court specifies otherwise.
 
• This power of judicial review is a key feature of democracies like India and the USA, ensuring the protection of **fundamental rights** and constitutional integrity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review:**

 
 
• It is the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions.
 
• Judicial review ensures that no law or government action violates the constitution.
 
• In India, this power is derived from Articles 13, 32, and 226 of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Unconstitutional Law:**
 
 
• A law is termed unconstitutional when it contravenes the provisions of the constitution, particularly fundamental rights.
 
• Such laws cannot be enforced and lose their legal validity.
 
 
 
• **Doctrine of Basic Structure:**
 
 
• The judiciary uses this doctrine to ensure that amendments or laws do not alter the basic framework of the constitution.
 
• This doctrine was established in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
 
 
 
• **Article 13 of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• Article 13 declares that any law inconsistent with the fundamental rights shall be void.
 
• It forms the basis for judicial review in India.

questions.question: What does OCI stand for in the context of Indian citizenship?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Overseas Citizen of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term **Overseas Citizen of India (OCI)** refers to a category of citizenship introduced by the Government of India for foreign nationals of Indian origin.
 
• OCI holders are eligible for a lifelong visa to visit India multiple times without requiring special permissions.
 
• The scheme was first introduced in **2005 under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act** to address the needs of the Indian diaspora.
 
• OCI cardholders enjoy several rights such as exemption from registration with the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) for any length of stay in India.
 
• However, OCI cardholders are not considered Indian citizens and do not have voting rights, employment in government positions, or access to agricultural property.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **OCI Card Eligibility:**

 
 
• Foreign nationals who were eligible to become Indian citizens on January 26, 1950, or belonged to a territory that became part of India after August 15, 1947, can apply.
 
• Children and grandchildren of such persons are also eligible, excluding those whose parents/grandparents hold citizenship of Pakistan or Bangladesh.
 
 
 
• **OCI Benefits:**
 
 
• OCI cardholders can access certain economic, financial, and educational privileges within India.
 
• They can work in private-sector jobs and access healthcare and educational facilities at par with Indian residents.
 
 
 
• **Restrictions for OCI Cardholders:**
 
 
• OCI cardholders cannot vote in Indian elections, hold public offices, or buy agricultural land.
 
• They are not allowed to work in government positions, including defense services.
 
 
 
• **OCI vs PIO:**
 
 
• OCI replaced the Person of Indian Origin (PIO) card scheme in 2015 to simplify diaspora benefits.
 
• Existing PIO cardholders were automatically converted to OCI cardholders.

questions.question: Free legal aid is part of which part of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Directive Principles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Free legal aid in India is enshrined under **Article 39A of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which emphasizes ensuring justice for all, particularly the weaker sections of society.
 
• The provision directs the state to **promote equal justice** and provide free legal aid to economically weaker sections to ensure no citizen is deprived of justice due to economic or other disabilities.
 
• The **Directive Principles** are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts but act as guiding principles for governance.
 
• This commitment towards free legal aid was further institutionalized through the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**, leading to the establishment of the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA).
 
• Free legal aid is a cornerstone of ensuring **access to justice**, a fundamental aspect of a welfare state as envisioned by the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are included in Part IV of the Indian Constitution and are drawn from the Irish Constitution.
 
• They aim to create a framework for a welfare state and guide the state in formulating policies that promote social and economic justice.
 
• While they are non-justiciable, they hold significant moral and political importance.
 
 
 
• **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987:**
 
 
• This Act was enacted to provide free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of society.
 
• It established the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) to oversee and implement free legal aid programs.
 
• Legal aid is provided for various categories, including women, children, SC/ST communities, and persons with disabilities.
 
 
 
• **Article 39A:**
 
 
• Article 39A was added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, and focuses on promoting equal justice and free legal aid.
 
• It upholds the principle of ensuring that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen based on economic or other disabilities.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights vs. Directive Principles:**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable and enforceable by courts, while DPSPs (Part IV) are non-justiciable.
 
• However, both are complementary, and the state is expected to balance them for achieving socio-economic justice.

questions.question: Which among the following significant changes was introduced in the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025?

Mandating representation of at least two Muslim women on Waqf Boards
Abolition of the Central Waqf Council

__
 
• The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 introduced a significant provision mandating the inclusion of **at least two Muslim women** in the composition of Waqf Boards across states and union territories.
 
• This amendment aimed to improve **gender representation** and ensure active participation of women in decision-making processes related to Waqf properties.
 
• The move aligns with India's broader agenda of **empowering women** and promoting inclusivity in administrative and religious domains.
 
• The amendment also emphasized **transparency** and accountability in the management of Waqf properties by diversifying board memberships.
 
• By mandating representation of Muslim women, the Act seeks to address **historical underrepresentation** of women in religious and property-related governance structures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: Which of the following Urban Local Government Bodies in India was discontinued after 1992?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Notified Area Committee**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Notified Area Committee (NAC)** was established in areas that were undergoing rapid urbanization but were yet to be declared municipalities.
 
• It was primarily **appointed by the state government** to manage urban administrative functions in newly urbanized regions.
 
• The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 introduced a uniform structure for urban local bodies, leading to the **discontinuation of the Notified Area Committee**.
 
• The amendment aimed to **streamline urban governance** by formalizing structures like Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• With the implementation of the 74th Amendment, urban governance was standardized, and NACs were replaced by **Nagar Panchayats or other urban local bodies**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992):**

 
 
• This amendment provided a **constitutional status** to urban local bodies and introduced a three-tier structure for urban governance: Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• It aimed to promote **decentralization and empower local governance**.
 
• The Act included provisions for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women in urban local bodies.
 
 
 
• **Municipal Corporation:**
 
 
• It is the **highest form of urban local government**, established in cities with large populations (typically over 1 million).
 
• Municipal Corporations are responsible for providing essential services like water supply, sanitation, waste management, and public health.
 
 
 
• **Municipal Council/Committee:**
 
 
• These are urban local bodies for smaller cities and towns with populations usually ranging between 20,000 and 1 million.
 
• They perform similar functions as Municipal Corporations but on a smaller scale.
 
 
 
• **Nagar Panchayat:**
 
 
• Nagar Panchayats are established in transitional areas where a **rural area is in the process of urbanizing**.
 
• They are tasked with basic urban planning and management for small urban settlements.

questions.question: What is the Gram Sabha in the context of the Panchayati Raj system in India?

options.text: An advisory council of State representatives
The deliberative assembly of all eligible village residents
A judicial body for urban areas

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The deliberative assembly of all eligible village residents**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Gram Sabha** refers to the assembly of all eligible voters in a village-level administrative unit within the Panchayati Raj system in India.
 
• It serves as a primary democratic institution, where decisions regarding village development, welfare activities, and local governance are deliberated upon.
 
• The Gram Sabha is responsible for approving the annual budget and development plans prepared by the Gram Panchayat.
 
• It ensures transparency and accountability in the functioning of the Gram Panchayat by allowing villagers to question and scrutinize its activities.
 
• As per Article 243A of the Indian Constitution, every Gram Sabha is a statutory body functioning at the village level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj System:**

 
 
• It is a decentralized form of governance in India, introduced through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992.
 
• It consists of three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), and Zilla Parishad (district level).
 
• The system aims to empower rural areas and ensure participatory democracy.
 
 
 
• **Article 243:**
 
 
• Articles 243 to 243-O in the Indian Constitution deal with the Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
• These articles provide the framework for the composition, powers, and functions of Panchayati Raj bodies.
 
 
 
• **Role of Gram Sabha:**
 
 
• It acts as a watchdog over the Gram Panchayat, ensuring transparency and accountability.
 
• The Gram Sabha can approve or reject plans, schemes, and budgets proposed by the Gram Panchayat.
 
• It provides a platform for villagers to voice their concerns and actively participate in governance.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Gram Sabha:**
 
 
• Promotes direct democracy at the grassroots level.
 
• Encourages participation from marginalized and underprivileged sections of society.
 
• Acts as a medium for collective decision-making on local issues.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a Notified Area Committee in India?

options.text: Oversee military areas to help address military and civilian issues
Manage developing towns due to get a municipality status
Handle port activities and ensure their smooth functioning
Regulate local elections for better local self-governance

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Manage developing towns due to get a municipality status**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A Notified Area Committee (NAC) is established to manage **fast-developing towns** that are yet to attain the status of a municipality in India.
 
• It is generally formed in regions with **industrial, commercial, or urban development** that require immediate governance and planning.
 
• The committee is appointed by the state government and does not have elected members, unlike municipal bodies.
 
• The NAC oversees **local infrastructure, sanitation, water supply, and urban planning** to facilitate organized growth.
 
• It acts as a transitional governance mechanism until the area formally qualifies for a municipal corporation or council status.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Municipality:**

 
 
• A municipality is a local governing body for urban areas, formed after an area meets specific population and development criteria set by the state.
 
• It is governed by elected representatives and is responsible for essential civic services like waste management, water supply, and urban infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Notified Area Committee vs Municipality:**
 
 
• While a municipality is an elected body, a Notified Area Committee is **appointed by the state government**.
 
• The NAC operates in areas experiencing rapid development where municipal governance is not yet feasible.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Towns:**
 
 
• Many notified areas are industrial hubs where accelerated growth demands administrative oversight to ensure sustainable urbanization.
 
• Examples include areas near ports, mines, or manufacturing facilities.
 
 
 
• **Urbanization in India:**
 
 
• India has witnessed rapid urbanization, with significant challenges in managing infrastructure, housing, and transportation.
 
• Governance mechanisms like NACs play a critical role in bridging the gap between rural and urban administrative needs.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India allowed citizens to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 19**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 19(1)(e)** of the Constitution of India provides citizens the fundamental right to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India.
 
• This right is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the State in the interest of the general public or for the protection of Scheduled Tribes.
 
• It ensures freedom of movement and residence across the country to promote national unity and integration.
 
• The provision is part of the broader framework of Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(5) may include measures for protecting indigenous tribal populations and maintaining public order.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are guaranteed under Part III of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They are enforceable by courts and are aimed at ensuring political and civil freedoms.
 
• Rights under Article 19 include freedom of speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession.
 
 
 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:**
 
 
• Rights under Article 19 are not absolute and can be restricted under Article 19(2) to 19(6).
 
• Restrictions are meant to safeguard public order, sovereignty, morality, and the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
 
 
 
• **Scheduled Tribes Protection:**
 
 
• Specific laws like the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution protect tribal areas and their autonomy.
 
• These laws aim to preserve the cultural and economic interests of indigenous tribal populations.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Amendments:**
 
 
• Amendments to Fundamental Rights require adherence to Article 368 of the Constitution.
 
• The judiciary plays a key role in interpreting these rights and ensuring they are not diluted arbitrarily.

questions.question: The power to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights is vested in the Supreme Court under which Article of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 32**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 32 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• Writs under Article 32 include Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto.
 
• It is often referred to as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, as described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, for safeguarding fundamental rights.
 
• This article provides the right to individuals to directly approach the Supreme Court in case of violation of their Fundamental Rights.
 
• The jurisdiction of Article 32 makes the Supreme Court the guardian and protector of Fundamental Rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Habeas Corpus:** A writ to produce a person before the court to ensure they are not detained unlawfully.
 
• **Mandamus:** A writ issued to a public official or body to perform a duty that they are legally obligated to fulfill.
 
• **Prohibition:** A writ issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction.
 
• **Certiorari:** A writ issued by a higher court to review the decision or proceedings of a lower court or tribunal.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** A writ to question the legality of a person holding a public office.
 
• Besides Article 32, High Courts are empowered to issue writs under Article 226, but the scope of Article 226 is wider as it includes not just Fundamental Rights but also other legal rights.
 
• The right to constitutional remedies, as provided under Article 32, is itself a Fundamental Right, ensuring citizens' access to justice.
 
• In certain situations, the enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32 may be suspended during the proclamation of Emergency under Article 359 of the Constitution.

questions.question: Lok Adalat proceedings are ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**conciliatory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lok Adalat proceedings are **non-adversarial and conciliatory**, aiming to resolve disputes amicably without prolonged litigation.
 
• It is governed under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which promotes alternative dispute resolution mechanisms.
 
• Lok Adalats encourage mutual agreement and compromise between disputing parties, ensuring faster and cost-effective justice.
 
• Decisions made in Lok Adalats are binding, and there is **no provision for appeal** against the award, ensuring finality of the resolution.
 
• This mechanism is particularly effective in resolving civil cases, matrimonial disputes, and minor criminal offenses, reducing the burden on regular courts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lok Adalat**:

 
 
• Lok Adalat translates to "People's Court" and is part of India's judicial system aimed at providing speedy justice.
 
• It operates under the **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)**.
 
• Cases resolved include disputes related to motor accident claims, family issues, and unpaid debts.
 
 
 
• **Conciliatory Proceedings**:
 
 
• Conciliation is a voluntary process where parties come to an agreement with the assistance of a neutral third party.
 
• It is less formal than mediation and involves facilitating communication between disputants.
 
 
 
• **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**:
 
 
• It provides the statutory basis for organizing Lok Adalats and ensuring legal aid to weaker sections of society.
 
• The Act aims to promote justice on the basis of equal opportunity.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Lok Adalats**:
 
 
• Ensures resolution without prolonged litigation, saving time and money.
 
• Encourages amicable settlements and reduces animosity between parties.
 
• Reduces the burden on conventional courts.

questions.question: How are Municipal Corporations established in the Union Territories of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By an Act of Parliament**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Municipal Corporations in Union Territories (UTs) are established **through Acts passed by the Parliament** of India, as UTs are governed directly by the Central Government.
 
• Unlike states, which have their own legislative assemblies, **Union Territories are administered by the President of India** through appointed administrators.
 
• The Parliament enacts laws to create and regulate municipal corporations in UTs, ensuring they fulfill the functions of urban local governance.
 
• For example, the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) operates under the **New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994**, passed by Parliament.
 
• This framework ensures consistency and uniformity in governance across UTs, considering their unique administrative structures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Municipal Corporation:**

 
 
• It is a form of urban local government that governs cities with a population exceeding 1 million.
 
• Municipal corporations are responsible for providing civic amenities such as water supply, waste management, roads, and public health services.
 
• They are governed by elected representatives (councillors) and an appointed municipal commissioner.
 
 
 
• **Union Territories:**
 
 
• Union Territories are regions in India directly governed by the Central Government.
 
• Currently, India has 8 Union Territories, including Delhi, Chandigarh, and Puducherry.
 
• Some UTs, like Delhi and Puducherry, have partial statehood with legislative assemblies.
 
 
 
• **New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC):**
 
 
• The NDMC is a municipal council governing the central area of New Delhi.
 
• It was constituted under the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, passed by Parliament.
 
• The council is chaired by a government-appointed officer, typically an IAS officer.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**
 
 
• The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, provides the framework for urban local governance in India.
 
• However, in Union Territories, Parliament has the authority to legislate municipal laws under Article 239 of the Constitution.

questions.question: What is the total full-time strength of personnels in the National Human Rights Commission, India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chairperson and five members**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India consists of a **Chairperson and five full-time members**.
 
• The Chairperson is typically a retired Chief Justice of India, ensuring the highest level of judicial oversight in human rights matters.
 
• The five members include **four full-time members** and one ex-officio member who serves as the Chairperson of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Minorities, and Women.
 
• The NHRC was established on **12 October 1993** under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
 
• It aims to protect and promote human rights in India, including rights related to life, liberty, equality, and dignity of individuals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Human Rights:**

 
 
• Human rights are fundamental rights that protect the dignity and freedom of individuals.
 
• They include rights such as freedom of speech, equality before the law, and protection against discrimination.
 
 
 
• **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993:**
 
 
• This act provides for the establishment of the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs).
 
• It outlines the powers and functions of the NHRC, including investigating human rights violations and recommending corrective measures.
 
 
 
• **Functions of NHRC:**
 
 
• Investigating complaints of human rights violations.
 
• Conducting inquiries, recommending reforms, and promoting awareness of human rights.
 
• It also reviews acts that may result in the violation of human rights and suggests remedies.
 
 
 
• **Composition of NHRC:**
 
 
• Chairperson: A retired Chief Justice of India.
 
• Four full-time members: Including individuals with judicial and human rights expertise.
 
• Ex-officio members from relevant commissions representing vulnerable sections of society.

questions.question: Which authority decides citizenship for people in newly added territories?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Union Government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Union Government is responsible for deciding citizenship in newly added territories to India as per the provisions of the Constitution and relevant laws.
 
• **Article 11** of the Indian Constitution **empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.**
 
• The Citizenship Act of 1955, enacted by the Union Government, lays out the legal framework for acquiring, renouncing, and determining citizenship in India.
 
• In cases where new territories are added to India, the Union Government decides citizenship based on the provisions outlined in the Citizenship Act.
 
• International agreements or treaties governing territorial addition may also influence citizenship decisions, which are implemented by the Union Government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 5-11 of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• These articles govern citizenship provisions in India.
 
• Article 11 explicitly empowers Parliament to make laws regulating citizenship.
 
 
 
• **The Citizenship Act, 1955:**
 
 
• It is the primary law governing citizenship in India.
 
• It includes provisions for citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
 
 
 
• **Incorporation of Territory:**
 
 
• When a new territory is added to India, its residents may be granted Indian citizenship based on legal provisions.
 
• The Union Government decides the criteria and implementation process for granting citizenship.
 
 
 
• **International Treaties and Agreements:**
 
 
• Territorial additions often occur due to international agreements or treaties.
 
• The Union Government ensures compliance with these agreements while determining citizenship for affected residents.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Oversight:**
 
 
• In case of disputes or challenges, the Supreme Court of India may interpret constitutional provisions related to citizenship.
 
• However, the primary authority remains with the Union Government.
